result:
There is a particular kind of silence that arrives just before rain. Birds pause. Leaves turn their pale undersides toward the sky. Even the traffic seems to move more carefully, as if the whole city has noticed something approaching.

Then the first drop falls—darkening the pavement with a mark no larger than a coin.

I like beginnings that are almost too small to notice. A raindrop. A sentence. A decision made while washing dishes. We tend to imagine change as something dramatic: doors slammed, trains boarded, declarations made beneath impossible weather. But most lives turn quietly. A person opens a book. Answers a message. Takes a different street home. Says yes where they usually say no.

Only later does the moment acquire a glow. Memory circles it and says, *There. That was when everything began.*

Perhaps that is why ordinary days deserve more attention. They are full of hidden hinges. The future is always entering through them, softly, without announcing its name.
